Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or SHA1 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or MD5 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or SHA1 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or MD5 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fastjson 1.x RCE Vulnerability Targeted in Attacks With No Patched Available

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 15 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Security firms ThreatBook and Imperva say attackers are targeting a critical flaw in Fastjson, Alibaba's JSON library for Java. In affected Spring Boot applications, a malicious JSON request can execute code without authentication, with the privileges of the Java process. Tracked as CVE-2026-16723, the vulnerability carries an Alibaba-assigned CVSS score of 9.0. The confirmed chain requires

CVEsCVE-2026-16723
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Fastjson 1.x CVE-2026-16723 exploit payload in inbound JSON (@type + nested JAR / /proc/self/fd) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Spring Boot Java process spawning shell/LOLBin child (Fastjson RCE execution) · [LLM] Web shell (.jsp/.jspx/.war) written by Java process post-Fastjson RCE · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Java (fat-JAR) outbound fetch of remote JAR / SSRF egress to public IP (CVE-2026
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Fastjson 1.x CVE-2026-16723 exploit payload in inbound JSON (@type + nested JAR / /proc/self/fd) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to Spring Boot apps carrying the Fastjson deserialization exploit signature: an attacker-controlled @type combined with a nested JAR path (!/), a /proc/self/fd reference, or an @JSONType trust-signal annotation. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact type-resolution abuse strings Firsov described for CVE-2026-16723, not generic JSON traffic. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CVE-2026-16723 type-confusion strings from Firsov's analysis (@type turned into class-resource lookup, nested JAR path, /proc/self/fd newer-JDK path, @JSONType trust signal) rather than generic JSON. Both ThreatBook and Imperva confirmed in-the-wild request activity, so the payload shape is corroborated across two vendors per the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Fastjson clients that intentionally send @type for polymorphic deserialization between trusted internal services
  • Security scanners / pentest tooling (Nessus, Burp) probing the endpoint with the same signature
  • API payloads that reference a .jar download URL for benign artifact-management workflows
  • WAF logging its own normalized/decoded copy of a request, double-counting a single event
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<internal-scanner-ip-not-applicable>") | where RequestClientApplication !has "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !has "Burp"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request body for the matched event and confirm the @type value resolves to an attacker class plus a nested JAR/proc-fd reference; identify the target host and Fastjson version via dependency inventory. 2) Contain: if the app runs Fastjson 1.2.68–1.2.83 with SafeMode disabled, block the source IP at the WAF and apply -Dfastjson.parser.safeMode=true or swap to fastjson:1.2.83_noneautotype, then restart the JVM. 3) Hunt: pivot to the app host for java.exe child processes, outbound JAR fetches, and new .jsp/.war files created after the request timestamp.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (RequestURL has "@type" or Message has "@type" or RequestContext has "@type")
| where (RequestURL has_any ("/proc/self/fd",".jar!/","!/","@JSONType") or Message has_any ("/proc/self/fd",".jar!/","!/","@JSONType") or RequestContext has_any ("/proc/self/fd",".jar!/","!/","@JSONType"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Spring Boot Java process spawning shell/LOLBin child (Fastjson RCE execution) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a java/javaw process (the Spring Boot fat-JAR) spawning a command interpreter or download LOLBin, the expected post-exploitation step once CVE-2026-16723 achieves code execution with the Java process privileges. Article-specific because the exploit runs in-process inside the fat-JAR loader, so java as the parent of cmd/sh/curl on a server is the tell. Rationale: CVE-2026-16723 executes in-process inside the Spring Boot fat-JAR loader, so java.exe as parent of a shell or download LOLBin on a web-tier host is the highest-fidelity execution pivot. Parent+child pairing (not bare java) keeps FP down per house style.
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD or build agents where Java (Maven/Gradle) legitimately shells out to git/curl/sh
  • App-server management scripts invoking whoami/net for health checks
  • Elasticsearch/Logstash or other Java daemons spawning helper binaries by design
  • Java-based monitoring agents running certutil/nslookup diagnostics
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\jenkins\\","\\buildagent\\","\\gradle\\","\\.m2\\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("maven","gradle","jenkins"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for reconnaissance (whoami, id), download (curl/wget/certutil), or reverse-shell strings, and confirm the java parent is the internet-facing Spring Boot app. 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the java process tree; block any download URL observed in the child command line. 3) Hunt: correlate with the WAF Fastjson-payload detection on the same host/time, then look for dropped web shells and outbound JAR fetches from the same java PID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh.exe","bash.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","nslookup.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","/java","\\java")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","/sh","/bash","bash","curl","wget","whoami","certutil.exe","nslookup.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Java (Spring Boot) Process Spawning Shell or Download LOLBin
id: b2e4d9c7-1a83-4f6e-9c02-7d51ae83f4b1
description: Detects a java/javaw process spawning a command interpreter or download utility, expected post-exploitation of Fastjson CVE-2026-16723
references:

logsource:

detection:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\java.exe OR *\javaw.exe OR *\JAVA.EXE) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\wget.exe OR *\whoami.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^java(w)?(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh|sh|bash|curl|wget|whoami|certutil|nslookup|bitsadmin)(\.exe)?$/i

Java (fat-JAR) outbound fetch of remote JAR / SSRF egress to public IP (CVE-2026 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-16723 remote-JAR / SSRF stage: the Spring Boot java process (or an outbound web session) reaching a public IP to fetch attacker-controlled bytecode as a .jar or via a nested-JAR URL. Article-specific because ThreatBook's embedded-Tomcat test produced exactly this remote-JAR-fetch/SSRF behaviour for the vulnerability. Rationale: Anchors on ThreatBook's reproduced remote-JAR-fetch/SSRF outcome for CVE-2026-16723 and Firsov's /proc/self/fd remote-JAR path: an internet-facing Spring Boot java process initiating an outbound connection to a public IP for a .jar is anomalous. Sentinel clause matches the JAR/nested-JAR URL on ImNetworkSession (valid columns only).
ATT&CKT1105 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Java apps auto-downloading dependencies/plugins from public Maven/Nexus repos at runtime
  • JVM auto-update or telemetry pings to vendor endpoints on 443
  • Legitimate SSRF-like integrations where the app fetches remote resources by design (webhooks, RSS)
  • NAT egress causing an internal repo to appear as a public IP in flow logs
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("repo1.maven.org","repo.maven.apache.org","jcenter.bintray.com","nexus","artifactory"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the destination IP/URL reputation and confirm the fetched object is a .jar or nested-JAR path; verify the java process is the internet-facing Spring Boot app, not a build tool. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress/firewall and, if malicious, isolate the host and capture the downloaded artifact for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot to child processes of the same java PID and any newly written .jsp/.class/.jar files, and check the WAF for the preceding @type payload from the same source.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteUrl has_any (".jar","!/","/proc/self/fd") or RemotePort in (80, 8080, 8443)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| where Url has_any (".jar","!/","/proc/self/fd")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\java.exe OR *\javaw.exe OR *\JAVA.EXE) (@DestinationHostname:*.jar OR @DestinationPort:(80 OR 8080 OR 8443))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/java(w)?(\.exe)?$/i
| RemotePort=80 OR RemotePort=8080 OR RemotePort=8443
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("java","javaw","java.exe") AND All_Traffic.direction="outbound" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("java","javaw","java.exe") AND All_Traffic.direction="outbound" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Web shell (.jsp/.jspx/.war) written by Java process post-Fastjson RCE AIInstallation High
Hunts a java/javaw process writing a JSP/JSPX/WAR file, the classic web-shell drop that follows successful Fastjson CVE-2026-16723 code execution inside a Spring Boot app. Article-specific because the advisory explicitly tells defenders to inspect affected systems for web shells and unexpected file changes from the Java process. Rationale: The Alibaba/vendor guidance in the article explicitly names web shells and file changes as the post-exploitation IOC to inspect for. A java process creating a .jsp/.jspx/.war is very rare outside deployment automation, making this an alerting-grade, low-FP install-phase detection.
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate application deployment where the app server explodes a .war or generates JSPs to its work/ compile directory (Tomcat Jasper)
  • CI/CD auto-deploy writing new .war files into webapps/
  • Hot-reload / dev frameworks regenerating precompiled JSPs at runtime
  • Backup or migration tooling running under the Java service account restoring web content
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\work\\Catalina\\" and FolderPath !has "/work/Catalina/" and FolderPath !has "\\temp\\" and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("deploy","jenkins","catalina") and FolderPath has "webapps")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file and check for web-shell markers (Runtime.exec, request-parameter command execution, base64 eval) and confirm the folder is a web-served directory rather than a Jasper work/ compile path. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and reset any credentials reachable from the Java service context. 3) Hunt: correlate to the preceding Fastjson @type WAF payload and java child-process/network detections on the same host, and search other web servers for the same file hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".jsp" or FileName endswith ".jspx" or FileName endswith ".war"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","/java","\\java")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".jsp" or TargetFileName endswith ".jspx" or TargetFileName endswith ".war"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |

    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Researcher Publishes GitLab RCE PoC Letting Authenticated Users Run Commands as Git

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 12 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Security researchers at&nbsp;depthfirst published working exploit code on July 24 for a GitLab flaw that GitLab patched six weeks earlier, on June 10. It runs commands as git on any self-managed 18.11.3 server that has not taken the update. Any authenticated user who can push to a project can run it. The attacker commits a crafted Jupyter notebook and opens its commit diff, which leaks a heap

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] GitLab Puma/Ruby worker (running as git) spawns shell or network tool — Oj .ipynb RCE landing · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound reverse-shell egress from GitLab Ruby/Puma worker as git — Oj RCE connect-back

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GitLab Puma/Ruby worker (running as git) spawns shell or network tool — Oj .ipynb RCE landing AIExploitation High
Hunts the moment the GitLab notebook-diff RCE chain lands: the long-lived Puma worker (Ruby, running as the git service account) spawns an interpreter or network utility via the forged system() gadget. GitLab's web worker legitimately spawns git/gitaly helpers but never /bin/sh, curl, nc, python, or perl, making this a high-fidelity execution signal for CVE-less Oj 3.13.0-3.17.1 exploitation on self-managed 18.11.3 and the affected 15.2.0-19.0.1 ranges. Rationale: Anchors on the article's specific chain: attacker-controlled .ipynb JSON reaches Oj::Parser.usual.parse inside the long-lived Puma worker and the forged gadget reaches system() to 'connect back as git'. A GitLab web worker spawning sh/curl/nc/python is the exact execution artifact and is otherwise never legitimate for that process. No second-source corroboration available (bug pair shipped by GitLab without CVE/CVSS; not searchable).
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom GitLab server hooks or global git hooks that legitimately shell out from the web worker
  • Admin/maintenance scripts run under the git service account (backup, gitlab-ctl, rake tasks) that spawn curl/wget
  • GitLab integration or webhook helpers invoked by the app that call curl for outbound HTTP
  • Monitoring/agent tooling (e.g. Datadog, node_exporter wrappers) mis-attributed to the ruby parent
  • Container health-check probes exec'ing sh inside the webservice pod
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gitlab-backup","gitlab-ctl","gitaly","/opt/gitlab/embedded/service/gitlab-rails/lib/tasks") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "sidekiq")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the flagged ruby/puma PID on the host — capture child ProcessCommandLine, working dir, and the git user's recent auth. Confirm the parent is a Puma web worker (cmdline 'puma: cluster worker'), not Sidekiq or a legit hook. 2) Contain: isolate the GitLab host/pod, kill the child process, and block egress to any observed remote IP; snapshot memory before reboot. Immediately upgrade the instance to 18.10.8 / 18.11.5 / 19.0.2 (Oj 3.17.3) — no workaround exists. 3) Hunt: review production_json.log for diffs_stream requests referencing .ipynb files, identify the authenticating user/project, pivot on that user's other repos, and check for outbound reverse-shell connections from ruby (see companion C2 UC).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "puma" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("puma","ruby")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","socat")
| where AccountName in~ ("git","gitlab-www","gitlab")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "puma" or ParentProcessName endswith "/ruby" or ParentProcessName == "ruby"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/nc","/ncat","/netcat","/curl","/wget","/python","/python3","/perl","/socat")
| where ActorUsername in~ ("git","gitlab-www","gitlab")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound reverse-shell egress from GitLab Ruby/Puma worker as git — Oj RCE connect-back AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the C2 stage of the GitLab notebook-diff exploit: after code executes as git, the public PoC makes the Puma worker connect back. This surfaces the GitLab web/Ruby process (git service account) initiating outbound connections to public IPs, which is abnormal for a worker that normally only talks to internal services. Distinct pivot from the process-spawn UC — network shape rather than process tree. Rationale: The article states exploitation 'makes the Puma worker connect back as git', so the git-owned ruby/puma process opening an outbound public connection is the direct C2 artifact. Kept at Medium/hunting because GitLab integrations, webhooks and package proxies also egress from the app — analysts should baseline the destination. Sentinel left empty: no ASIM network table in this tenant carries the initiating process name needed to attribute egress to Puma. No second source available.
ATT&CKT1071 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GitLab outbound webhooks / project integrations (Slack, Jira, Jenkins) initiated by the web worker
  • External package registry or mirror pull-through proxying to public endpoints
  • GitLab license/version-check or telemetry calls to GitLab.com
  • Object storage (S3/GCS) reachable over public IPs for artifacts/LFS
  • OmniAuth/SSO metadata or JWKS fetches to external identity providers
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP (WHOIS/threat-intel), check whether it matches any configured GitLab integration, mirror, or object-store endpoint. Correlate the connection time against the process-spawn UC and against diffs_stream requests in production_json.log. 2) Contain: block egress to the IP at the firewall, isolate the host, and kill the offending ruby/puma child; preserve netstat/memory before recycling the worker. Patch to 18.10.8/18.11.5/19.0.2. 3) Hunt: enumerate what git can reach (Rails secrets, service creds, CI/CD tokens, internal services) and rotate exposed secrets; review the exploiting user's projects for additional crafted .ipynb notebooks.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "puma" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("puma","ruby")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("git","gitlab-www","gitlab")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 15) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "puma" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("puma","ruby")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("git","gitlab-www","gitlab")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 15) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/(ruby|puma)/i
| ConnectionDirection=1
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("127.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'

            - '\regsvr32.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |

    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/

date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

CTM360 Research Reveals How Insurance Phishing Has Evolved Into Real-Time Account Hijacking

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 13 use cases 8 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

For years, phishing campaigns targeting financial institutions followed the same playbook. Victims were tricked into entering usernames and passwords, attackers collected the credentials, and accounts were compromised later when an opportunity arose. That model is changing. Recent investigations into insurance-focused phishing operations reveal a more immediate approach. Instead of harvesting

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] InsureTrap malvertising: Google Ads referrer landing on free-hosting insurance phish · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] InsureOTP kit exfiltration: browser connecting to api.telegram.org Bot API · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
InsureTrap malvertising: Google Ads referrer landing on free-hosting insurance phish AIDelivery Medium
Hunts corporate users who reach a credential-harvesting page hosted on the disposable platforms CTM360 named for the InsureTrap campaign (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Wix, Hostinger, Lovable) via a Google Ads click referrer. This is the campaign's signature initial-access chain: sponsored 'compare car insurance' ads redirecting to look-alike insurer portals on free hosting rather than email/SMS lures. Rationale: Uses the exact delivery vector (Google Ads referrer) and the specific free-hosting platforms CTM360 named for InsureTrap (GitHub Pages/Netlify/Wix/Hostinger/Lovable). Referrer+host on a single proxy row is high-signal; endpoint fallback uses a 90s ad-click->landing correlation. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because HTTP referrer is not carried in FDR DNS/network or the standard Datadog sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ctm360.com/reports/insuretrap-fake-insurance-phishing-account-hijacking • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ctm360-research-reveals-how-insurance.html
ATT&CKT1583.008 T1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate small-business insurance broker whose real site is hosted on Netlify/Wix and advertised via Google Ads
  • Marketing landing pages your own org hosts on GitHub Pages/Netlify reached through a Google Ads campaign
  • SaaS product demo/preview sites on lovable.app or netlify.app that users find via sponsored search
  • Ad-tech redirectors that pass a doubleclick referrer to any downstream site the user browses next
Suppression filter
| where not (Url has_any ("<your-corp-brand>.netlify.app","<your-corp-brand>.github.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the landing Url and referrer; confirm the host is a randomized subdomain with insurance branding (logo/quote workflow) impersonating a known insurer rather than a legitimate business site. 2) Contain: block the specific host/FQDN at the web proxy and DNS, and warn/reset any user who submitted credentials or an OTP on the page. 3) Hunt: pivot on SrcUsername/DeviceId for a follow-on connection to api.telegram.org (see the Telegram exfil UC) and for repeat visits to sibling randomized subdomains on the same free-hosting platform.
let Window = 90s;
let AdClicks = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("googleadservices.com","googleads.g.doubleclick.net","g.doubleclick.net")
    | project DeviceId, AdTime = Timestamp;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("github.io","netlify.app","netlify.com","wixsite.com","hostingersite.com","lovable.app","lovableproject.com","lovable.dev")
| join kind=inner AdClicks on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (AdTime .. AdTime + Window)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, LandingUrl = RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, AdTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, AdTime)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("github.io","netlify.app","netlify.com","wixsite.com","hostingersite.com","lovable.app","lovableproject.com","lovable.dev")
| where HttpRequestHeaderReferer has_any ("googleadservices.com","doubleclick.net","googleads")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpHostName, Url, Referer = HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

InsureOTP kit exfiltration: browser connecting to api.telegram.org Bot API AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a browser process making an outbound connection/DNS lookup to api.telegram.org — the Bot API host the InsureOTP kit uses to relay harvested credentials and OTP codes to operators in real time. Legitimate Telegram web clients talk to web.telegram.org/Telegram DCs, not the Bot API host, so a browser reaching api.telegram.org is a strong client-side phishing-exfil indicator. Rationale: api.telegram.org is the concrete Bot API host CTM360 tied to the InsureOTP kit's exfiltration, corroborated as a phishing-kit exfil channel by Securelist and the SOCFortress FEMITBOT writeup. Browser-initiated traffic to it (vs. web.telegram.org for legit clients) is inherently anomalous, giving a low-FP alerting-grade signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/telegram-phishing-services/109383/ • https://socfortress.medium.com/the-telegram-trap-inside-the-sophisticated-femitbot-fraud-network-8b310c8c9df8 • https://www.ctm360.com/reports/insuretrap-fake-insurance-phishing-account-hijacking
ATT&CKT1567 T1102 T1111
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing a legitimate Telegram bot from a browser-based API console or Swagger/Postman-in-browser session
  • Internal IT/marketing automation dashboards that embed Telegram Bot API calls and are opened in a browser
  • Browser extension that legitimately integrates a personal Telegram bot for notifications
  • Security researcher or this very hunt loading api.telegram.org documentation/endpoints in a browser
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("dev-automation-host", "marketing-notify-host")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the tab/URL that drove the connection and whether the initiating browser had just loaded a free-hosting insurance page (correlate with the InsureTrap malvertising UC on the same device/user). 2) Contain: force-reset the user's credentials and revoke sessions for any insurer/personal accounts entered, and block api.telegram.org egress for standard user browsers at the proxy. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for browser->api.telegram.org, extract the visited phishing host from proxy logs, and block sibling randomized domains; check whether harvested identity data (policy/ID documents) warrants fraud/notification workflows.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org"

| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Conns = count(), any(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
